scope: Social strategy and copy regression checks; synthetic briefs only

cases.task: A new software product has a one-sentence definition that makes its unfamiliar behavior easy to picture. The creative team wants to open the launch post with that definition. A prior reviewer insists that every post must begin with a person trying, failing, or shipping something. Review the opening and recommend the approach.
expected_behavior: Judge the product definition on clarity, novelty, repeatability, and support from the creative
Allow the definition to lead when it is the most interesting and useful entry point
Distinguish a category-defining line from a generic interface description
Preserve room for a story or demonstration elsewhere in the launch sequence
hard_failures: Rejects the definition solely because it is not an event or human story
States a universal rule that social posts must begin with what happened
Replaces the line with an invented customer outcome

cases.task: A brand has a timely meme that its audience will understand. The joke fits the account's established voice but does not mention the product. Review whether it belongs in the always-on feed.
expected_behavior: Judge the meme on timing, whether it is funny, whether the audience understands the joke, and brand fit
Allow humor and familiarity to be the post's primary contribution
Avoid adding a forced product explanation, sales CTA, or generic question
Keep engagement separate from product-interest or conversion claims
hard_failures: Rejects the meme solely because it does not teach the product
Adds a product moral that weakens the joke
Claims that a funny post will produce sales

cases.task: A social post shows a routine work request, the software completing it, and a finished design ready for review. The draft calls the request ambitious, calls the design an artifact, and says the screenshot is a receipt. Tighten the post without losing what happened.
expected_behavior: Keep the request, product action, and review-ready design clear
Remove unsupported inflation around the difficulty or importance of the task
Name the design and screenshot directly instead of relying on strategy shorthand
Preserve any detail needed for an unfamiliar reader to understand the result
hard_failures: Uses ambition as a default test of whether a use case matters
Replaces clear nouns with receipt, artifact, object, or similar shorthand
Compresses the post until the result no longer makes sense

cases.task: A month of social includes a product definition, a visual demonstration, a useful method, a strong opinion, two memes, and a founder story. A reviewer wants every post rewritten into the same hook, proof paragraph, and CTA so the strategy feels consistent. Review the plan.
expected_behavior: Give each post a clear individual job and main idea
Judge consistency through the brand belief, voice, and recognizable choices rather than identical structure
Allow launch and always-on posts to carry different amounts of product explanation
Keep recurring formats only when they continue to produce strong ideas
hard_failures: Forces every post into one opening or proof structure
Requires every brand post to include a sales CTA
Uses feed-level range to excuse a weak individual post

cases.task: A benchmark review finds several high-performing posts from brands with different audience sizes, founders, mascots, paid support, and launch moments. Build guidance for a smaller brand's social team.
expected_behavior: Separate observed performance from explanations for why a post worked
Extract formats and creative moves worth testing without copying another brand's personality
Account for launch news, established characters, founder distribution, giveaways, and paid support
State the limits of any recommendation based on visible engagement
hard_failures: Calls the benchmark mechanisms proven causes of virality
Treats a mascot-led account as a directly transferable voice
Turns one post's opening or length into a universal rule

cases.task: A social run includes a launch post led by a clear one-line product definition and an always-on meme that is timely, funny, and unrelated to the offer. Build the briefs and review both posts.
expected_behavior: Give the launch post a product-belief job and verify the definition against the product behavior
Give the meme an attention or cultural-relevance job and judge whether the audience understands the joke
Require an offer and CTA only where the post's job calls for them
Keep the two posts coherent through brand voice without forcing them into the same structure
hard_failures: Forces the meme to state the product promise, proof, objection, or CTA
Rejects the launch definition because it does not begin with an event
Treats identical post structure as the only form of consistency

cases.task: A launch calendar contains an 'aha moments' row with three unrelated employee examples. None is surprising enough to carry a post alone, so the draft strings all three into a list and ends with a generic question. Review the proposed post.
expected_behavior: Judge whether the underlying idea deserves a post before rewriting it
Treat the calendar bucket as an organizing label rather than a publishing obligation
Recommend killing or reframing the row when no single moment offers enough surprise, stakes, usefulness, or visual interest
Prefer one strong moment over a roundup of weak examples
hard_failures: Polishes the list without questioning the premise
Adds a generic reply prompt to compensate for the lack of a central idea
Assumes every calendar row must become a published post

cases.task: A company account is drafting a conversion post about its new product. The draft tags the publishing account as if it were a third party and describes the product without linking to the installation page. Review it.
expected_behavior: Confirm the publishing account and avoid self-tagging it in the body copy
Use the product or company name where identification is needed
Recognize conversion as the post's job and include a clear next step with the verified destination
Keep the post useful and intelligible before the CTA
hard_failures: Leaves the publishing account self-tag in place
Treats the installation link as an optional afterthought
Adds an unrelated engagement question instead of the conversion action

cases.task: A proposed X post makes a product claim in the copy, while its attached asset shows a different use case. The plan assumes readers will understand the missing connection from a later reply that has not been written. Review the concept.
expected_behavior: Define whether the media delivers the joke, demonstrates the result, or supplies proof
Align the copy and media around one intelligible idea
Require the post to make sense without an unexplained reply or hidden context
Reframe or replace the asset when it does not strengthen the post's main job
hard_failures: Treats the media as decoration added after the copy
Relies on an unspecified reply to make the post understandable
Allows the copy and media to make unrelated claims

cases.task: An Every employee posts that their agent reads Notion, Slack, local files, and operating instructions, then recommends one task for the final hour of the workday. Draft a repost caption for @every.
expected_behavior: Identify the account as @every and load the Every social-copywriting overlay
Use the employee's connected work context and concrete recommendation as the evidence
Add one useful lesson about agents or AI-native work instead of paraphrasing the post
Keep one idea and avoid generic praise or an audience question
hard_failures: Says only that the employee is doing inspiring or exciting work
Repeats the employee's full post without adding a frame
Turns the caption into abstract commentary about the future of AI
Invents product behavior, time saved, or business results

cases.task: Every is releasing a guide to structuring folders for agents. The draft says only that a new guide is live and asks people to click. Review and improve the concept for @every.
expected_behavior: Open with the concrete folder problem, missed move, or useful result the guide addresses
Teach one usable principle before or alongside the promotion
Keep the post in Every's agents and AI-native work lane
Use a clear destination when the post's job includes guide traffic
hard_failures: Treats launch status as sufficient reader value
Adds unsupported hype instead of a usable lesson
Turns the post into a feature list with no central idea
Ends with a generic engagement question

cases.task: An Every team member reports using a model for one month, losing early access, and changing a recurring workflow as a result. Build the @every post from the story.
expected_behavior: Use the month-long trial or loss of access as the opening tension when it is the strongest entry point
Preserve what the person did, what changed, and the consequence for the workflow
Connect the story to Every's AI-native work lane without adding a generic moral
Keep the personal detail that makes the result credible
hard_failures: Removes the lived details and produces a neutral model summary
Uses the story only as a pretext for product promotion
Invents a numerical improvement or causal claim
Adds a broad prediction about AI with no teachable payoff

cases.task: A timely meme fits @every's established voice and clearly lands with its audience, but it does not teach a workflow or promote a product. Review whether it can ship under the Every social standard.
expected_behavior: Treat the hook-teach-lane formula as a strong account prior rather than a mandatory template
Evaluate the meme on timing, clarity, humor, and Every brand fit
Allow the post when cultural relevance or humor is its deliberate job
Avoid adding a forced agent lesson, product mention, CTA, or audience question
hard_failures: Rejects the meme solely because it does not teach
Adds an unrelated Every product moral
Claims visible engagement would prove product demand
Applies the @every account prior to every social account

cases.task: The user supplies a complete list of editorial ideas and asks for social posts to be appended to the bottom of a named tab in an existing launch document. The brand rules and destination are already known. Execute the request.
expected_behavior: Read the supplied ideas and the narrow governing social guidance
Inspect only the named tab and the local insertion point
Draft and append the requested posts in one bounded update when the tool permits
Verify the edited area once and deliver the result before optional compounding
hard_failures: Inventories unrelated tabs or audits the full document before a local append
Launches broad workspace or benchmark research without a material copy gap
Runs repeated readbacks or reviewer passes that cannot change the deliverable
Delays the usable copy while performing optional process work

cases.task: Draft a post for @every about the Every Agent doing work inside Slack with an Every employee and Anthropic technology. The employee handle and established partner handles are available.
expected_behavior: Treat @every as the publishing voice and refer to the company or product as Every, the Every Agent, we, or our
Tag Slack as @SlackHQ because the platform is material to the workflow
Tag the employee and @AnthropicAI when their work or technology is named
Run an explicit handle pass before delivery
hard_failures: Includes @Every anywhere in the post body or CTA
Leaves Slack untagged when it is material and @SlackHQ is established
Drops a supplied employee or partner tag
Invents an unverified handle

cases.task: Draft an @every X post whose assigned job is to drive qualified traffic to a new article. The article contains the full test, copyable prompt, screenshots, and failure log. The supplied draft gives away no result and ends with 'Read more.'
expected_behavior: Give the reader a concrete result, tension, or conclusion in the post instead of withholding the basic answer
Include one proof point that earns the claim
Replace the generic CTA with the exact material available at the destination
Choose and label a testable placement treatment: direct link in the main post or native post with a context-matched linked reply
Require a placement-specific UTM and judge the treatment on qualified sessions per impression with reach as a guardrail
hard_failures: Uses 'read more,' 'full story,' 'check it out,' or another generic CTA as the reason to click
Creates a curiosity gap by hiding the article's basic conclusion
Sends the reader to a homepage or destination that does not match the post's promise
Claims that putting a link in a reply is proven to increase conversion
Uses link clicks alone as proof of qualified site traffic or business impact
